Suppose that $0 \in x \boxplus y \boxplus z$. Does it then follow that \[     0 \in x^3 \boxplus y^3 \boxplus z^3 \boxplus -xyz \boxplus -xyz \boxplus -xyz\text{?} \] end{Ques}

Yes. The implication holds for every hyperfield. The key point is that a classical theorem of Krasner says that every hyperfield is a quotient of a field by a subgroup of its multiplicative group; then the statement lifts to the ordinary field identity
\[
X^3+Y^3+Z^3-3XYZ=(X+Y+Z)(X^2+Y^2+Z^2-XY-YZ-ZX).
\]
Relevant background on hyperfields and quotient/dequantization constructions includes
[ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2307.09400),
[ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1006.3034),
[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.17302), and
[math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/%7Eoleg/VersoTeX/Show/Hyperfields/hf.html).

Below is a compilable LaTeX document containing a complete proof, with the representation theorem cited carefully.

```latex
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{amssymb}
\usepackage{amsthm}
\usepackage{hyperref}

\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}
\newtheorem{lemma}[theorem]{Lemma}
\newtheorem{definition}[theorem]{Definition}
\newtheorem{remark}[theorem]{Remark}

\title{A cubic zero-sum implication for hyperfields}
\author{}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section*{Notation and conventions}

Let \(\mathbb H\) be a hyperfield with multivalued addition \(\boxplus\), additive identity \(0\), and multiplicative identity \(1\). For the definition of hyperfields and the extension of \(\boxplus\) to finite strings and subsets, see for instance
\href{https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2307.09400}{ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org}
and
\href{https://arxiv.org/html/2309.17302}{arxiv.org}.
For \(a\in\mathbb H\), \(-a\) denotes the unique additive inverse of \(a\), i.e.\ the unique element satisfying
\[
0\in a\boxplus(-a).
\]
In the expression \(-xyz\), the minus sign applies to the product: \(-xyz=-(xyz)\).

Repeated hyperaddition is understood associatively, as usual; equivalently one may flatten repeated hyperadditions using the power-set monad, as in
\href{https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2307.09400}{ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org}.

We shall prove the following theorem.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
Let \(\mathbb H\) be a hyperfield, and let \(x,y,z\in\mathbb H\). Suppose
\[
0\in x\boxplus y\boxplus z.
\]
Then
\[
0\in x^3\boxplus y^3\boxplus z^3\boxplus(-(xyz))\boxplus(-(xyz))\boxplus(-(xyz)).
\]
\end{theorem}

The proof uses Krasner's representation theorem for hyperfields and a lifting argument to an ordinary field.

\section{Quotient hyperfields}

\begin{definition}\label{def:quotient-hyperfield}
Let \(F\) be a field and let \(G\le F^\times\) be a subgroup of its multiplicative group. Write
\[
F/G:=\{0\}\cup F^\times/G.
\]
Multiplication is defined by
\[
0\cdot A=0,\qquad (aG)(bG)=abG.
\]
Hyperaddition is defined as follows. For nonzero cosets \(A=aG\) and \(B=bG\),
\[
A\boxplus B
=
\{\,cG\in F^\times/G : \exists \alpha\in A,\ \beta\in B\text{ with }\alpha+\beta=c\,\},
\]
and \(0\in A\boxplus B\) precisely when there exist \(\alpha\in A,\beta\in B\) with \(\alpha+\beta=0\). Also
\[
0\boxplus A=A\boxplus 0=\{A\},\qquad 0\boxplus 0=\{0\}.
\]
This is the usual quotient hyperfield construction; see
\href{https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1006.3034}{ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org}
and
\href{https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/\%7Eoleg/VersoTeX/Show/Hyperfields/hf.html}{math.stonybrook.edu}.
\end{definition}

The following lifting property is elementary but crucial.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:lift-zero-sum}
Let \(F/G\) be a quotient hyperfield, and let \(A_1,\dots,A_n\in F/G\). Then
\[
0\in A_1\boxplus\cdots\boxplus A_n
\]
if and only if there exist representatives \(a_i\in A_i\) such that
\[
a_1+\cdots+a_n=0
\]
in the field \(F\). Here if \(A_i=0\), the only representative is \(a_i=0\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For \(n=1\), the statement is clear. For \(n=2\), it is exactly the definition of hyperaddition in a quotient hyperfield.

Assume the result for \(n-1\). If
\[
0\in A_1\boxplus\cdots\boxplus A_n,
\]
then by associativity of hyperaddition there is some
\[
B\in A_1\boxplus\cdots\boxplus A_{n-1}
\]
such that \(0\in B\boxplus A_n\). By the case \(n=2\), there exist \(b\in B\) and \(a_n\in A_n\) with \(b+a_n=0\). By the induction hypothesis applied to \(B\), there exist \(a_i\in A_i\) for \(1\le i\le n-1\) such that
\[
a_1+\cdots+a_{n-1}=b.
\]
Thus
\[
a_1+\cdots+a_{n-1}+a_n=0.
\]

Conversely, suppose \(a_i\in A_i\) and \(a_1+\cdots+a_n=0\). Put \(b=a_1+\cdots+a_{n-1}\). By the induction hypothesis,
\[
b\in A_1\boxplus\cdots\boxplus A_{n-1}.
\]
Since \(b+a_n=0\), the definition of quotient hyperaddition gives
\[
0\in b\boxplus A_n.
\]
Hence
\[
0\in A_1\boxplus\cdots\boxplus A_n.
\]
\end{proof}

\section{Krasner's representation theorem}

We use the following classical theorem of Krasner. Expositions and discussions of this result can be found in
\href{https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1006.3034}{ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org},
\href{https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2307.09400}{ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org},
and
\href{https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/\%7Eoleg/VersoTeX/Show/Hyperfields/hf.html}{math.stonybrook.edu}.

\begin{theorem}[Krasner]\label{thm:krasner}
Every hyperfield \(\mathbb H\) is isomorphic to a quotient hyperfield \(F/G\), where \(F\) is a field and \(G\le F^\times\) is a subgroup of its multiplicative group.
\end{theorem}

Thus, without loss of generality, one may prove universal hyperfield identities by working in a quotient hyperfield \(F/G\), provided the argument uses only the hyperfield operations and their quotient description.

\section{The field identity}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:field-identity}
Let \(F\) be a field, and let \(X,Y,Z\in F\) satisfy
\[
X+Y+Z=0.
\]
Then
\[
X^3+Y^3+Z^3+(-XYZ)+(-XYZ)+(-XYZ)=0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
X^3+Y^3+Z^3-3XYZ=0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
In the polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[X,Y,Z]\), one has the universal identity
\[
X^3+Y^3+Z^3-3XYZ
=
(X+Y+Z)(X^2+Y^2+Z^2-XY-YZ-ZX).
\]
Reducing coefficients in the field \(F\), the same identity holds in \(F[X,Y,Z]\). If \(X+Y+Z=0\), the right-hand side is \(0\), hence
\[
X^3+Y^3+Z^3-3XYZ=0.
\]
But in the field \(F\),
\[
-3XYZ=(-XYZ)+(-XYZ)+(-XYZ),
\]
so the desired equality follows.
\end{proof}

\section{Proof of the main theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]
By Krasner's representation theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:krasner}), there exist a field \(F\), a subgroup \(G\le F^\times\), and a hyperfield isomorphism
\[
\phi:\mathbb H\longrightarrow F/G.
\]
Write
\[
A=\phi(x),\qquad B=\phi(y),\qquad C=\phi(z).
\]
Since \(\phi\) preserves hyperaddition and \(0\), the hypothesis gives
\[
0\in A\boxplus B\boxplus C.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:lift-zero-sum}, there exist representatives
\[
X\in A,\qquad Y\in B,\qquad Z\in C
\]
such that
\[
X+Y+Z=0
\]
in \(F\).

By Lemma~\ref{lem:field-identity},
\[
X^3+Y^3+Z^3+(-XYZ)+(-XYZ)+(-XYZ)=0.
\]
Now observe that:
\begin{itemize}
\item \(X^3\in A^3=\phi(x^3)\);
\item \(Y^3\in B^3=\phi(y^3)\);
\item \(Z^3\in C^3=\phi(z^3)\);
\item \(-XYZ\in -(ABC)=\phi(-(xyz))\).
\end{itemize}
Indeed, multiplication in \(F/G\) is induced by multiplication in \(F\), and additive inverses in \(F/G\) are represented by negatives in \(F\).

Therefore, applying Lemma~\ref{lem:lift-zero-sum} to the six hyperfield elements
\[
A^3,\ B^3,\ C^3,\ -(ABC),\ -(ABC),\ -(ABC),
\]
we obtain
\[
0\in
A^3\boxplus B^3\boxplus C^3
\boxplus (-(ABC))\boxplus (-(ABC))\boxplus (-(ABC)).
\]
Finally, since \(\phi\) is a hyperfield isomorphism, pulling back by \(\phi^{-1}\) yields
\[
0\in
x^3\boxplus y^3\boxplus z^3
\boxplus (-(xyz))\boxplus (-(xyz))\boxplus (-(xyz)).
\]
This proves Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The argument shows that the implication is not a special feature of any particular hyperfield; it is a consequence of Krasner's representation theorem together with the classical polynomial identity over fields. In the terminology sometimes used in the literature, this says that every hyperfield is \emph{perfect} with respect to this cubic relation.
\end{remark}

\begin{thebibliography}{9}

\bibitem{Factoring}
Factoring multivariate polynomials over hyperfields and the multivariable Descartes' problem,
\href{https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2307.09400}{ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org}.

\bibitem{Viro}
Hyperfields for Tropical Geometry I. Hyperfields and dequantization,
\href{https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1006.3034}{ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org}.

\bibitem{TropicalExtensions}
Geometry of tropical extensions of hyperfields,
\href{https://arxiv.org/html/2309.17302}{arxiv.org}.

\bibitem{StonyBrook}
Hyperfields and dequantization, lecture notes/web page,
\href{https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/\%7Eoleg/VersoTeX/Show/Hyperfields/hf.html}{math.stonybrook.edu}.

\end{thebibliography}

\end{document}

url_citation.content:
A hyperfield is a tuple $H=(H,0,1,\cdot,\boxplus)$ where

...

$H^{*}=(H\setminus\{0\},1,\cdot)$ is an Abelian group,

...

$0$ is an absorbing element: $0\cdot a=a\cdot 0$ for all $a\in H$ .

...

Additionally, the hyperaddition $\boxplus$ is a multivalued operation, that is a function $\boxplus\colon H\times H\to\{\text{nonempty subsets of }H\}$ , such that for all $a,b\in H$ :

...

•

...

$a\boxplus b=b\boxplus a$ (commutative),

...

•

...

$0\boxplus a=\{a\}$ (identity),

•

...

there is a unique element $-a$ such that $0\in a\boxplus(-a)$ (inverses),

...

•

...

$\bigcup\{a\boxplus t:t\in b\boxplus c\}=\bigcup\{t\boxplus c:t\in a\boxplus b\}$ (associative)

•

...

$a\in b\boxplus c\iff-b\in(-a)\boxplus c$ (reversible)

...

Repeated addition is treated monadically, using the power set monad. This means that notationally we will identify elements of $H$ and singletons and repeated hyperaddition is flattened by unions—for example, $a\boxplus(b\boxplus c)=(a\boxplus b)\boxplus c$ means exactly what the associativity axiom says.

###### Theorem 3.A.

...

(Cf. Marshall [10] ) A set \(X\) with a multivalued operation \((a,b)\mapsto a\cdot b\) is a multigroup iff there exist a map \(X\to X:a\mapsto a^{-1}\) and an element \(1\in X\) such that: 

 (1') \((a\cdot b)\cdot c\subset a\cdot (b\cdot c)\) for any \(a,b,c\in X\), 

 (2') \(a\cdot 1=a\) for any \(a\in X\), 

 (3') Reversibility property. \(c\in a\cdot b\) implies \(a\in c\cdot b^{-1}\) and \(b\in a^{-1}\cdot c\) for \(a,b,c\in X\).

...

#### Proof. 

 This theorem claims that in a hyperfield distributivity holds in a strong form: \(a(b\tplus c)= (ab)\tplus (ac)\). Indeed, the inclusion \(a(b\tplus c)\subset (ab)\tplus (ac)\) that holds true in multirings implies the opposite inclusion if \(a\ne 0\): 

 \[(ab)\tplus (ac)=a^{-1}a((ab)\tplus (ac))\subset a(a^{-1}ab\tplus a^{-1}ac)=a(b\tplus b).\] 

 For \(a=0\), the equality \(a(b\tplus c)= (ab)\tplus (ac)\) holds true since both sides are equal to \(0\).

...

For example, in a usual ring, distributivity implies that \((a+b)(x+y)=ax+ay+bx+by\). In a multiring and even in a hyperfield the proof fails. Moreover, the equality 

 \[(a\tplus b)(x\tplus y)=ax\tplus ay\tplus bx\tplus by\] 

 may be incorrect, see Sections 5.1 , 6.4 .

...

Let us analyze, why the arguments that deduce \((a+b)(x+y)=ax+ay+bx+by\) from distributivity for univalued addition do not work for multivalued addition. In the univalued case, \(x+y\) is just an element, and one can apply distributivity: \((a+b)(x+y)=a(x+y)+b(x+y)\). Then for each summand distributivity is applied again, giving the equality.

...

In the case of multivalued addition \(\tplus \), \((x\tplus y)\) is not an element, but a set. Therefore the distributivity \((a\tplus b)c=ac\tplus bc\), in which \(c\) is a single element (that is an axiom in a multiring) cannot be applied in the situation when \(c\) is a set \(x\tplus y\).

...

###### Theorem 4.B. 

 In any multiring, \((a\tplus b)(x\tplus y)\subset ax\tplus ay\tplus bx\tplus by\). 

 For each element \(c\in (x\tplus y)\) the distributivity gives \((a\tplus b)c=ac\tplus bc\), and we get 

 \[(a\tplus b)(x\tplus y)= \bigcup _{c\in (x\tplus y)}(a\tplus b)c= \bigcup _{c\in (x\tplus y)}(ac\tplus bc).\] 

 On the other hand, 

 \[ ax\tplus ay\tplus bx\tplus by= (ax\tplus ay)\tplus (bx\tplus by)=\\ a(x\tplus y)\tplus b(x\tplus y)\supset ac\tplus bc \] 

 for any \(c\in (x\tplus y)\), and therefore 

 \[ax\tplus bx\tplus ay\tplus by\supset \bigcup _{c\in (x\tplus y)}(ac\tplus bc)=(a\tplus b)(x\tplus y). \]

Given a set $ℍ{\mathbb{H}}$, we denote the set of non-empty subsets of $ℍ{\mathbb{H}}$ by $𝒫∗​(ℍ){\mathcal{P}}^{*}({\mathbb{H}})$. A hyperoperation on $ℍ{\mathbb{H}}$ is a map $⊞:ℍ×ℍ→𝒫∗​(ℍ)\boxplus\colon{\mathbb{H}}\times{\mathbb{H}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{P}}^{*}({\mathbb{H}})$ that sends two elements $a,b∈ℍa,b\in{\mathbb{H}}$ to a non-empty subset $a⊞ba\boxplus b$ of $ℍ{\mathbb{H}}$. This map can be extended to strings of elements, or sums of subsets, via:

...

$a1⊞a2⊞⋯⊞ak\displaystyle a_{1}\boxplus a_{2}\boxplus\dots\boxplus a_{k}$

...

For ease of notation, we shall refrain from using set brackets for singleton sets. The hyperoperation $⊞\boxplus$ is called associative if it satisfies

...

$(a⊞b)⊞c=a⊞(b⊞c),∀a,b,c∈ℍ,(a\boxplus b)\boxplus c=a\boxplus(b\boxplus c)\quad,\quad\forall a,b,c\in{\mathbb{H}}\,,$

...

and is called commutative if it satisfies

...

$a⊞b=b⊞a∀a,b∈ℍ.a\boxplus b=b\boxplus a\quad\forall a,b\in{\mathbb{H}}\,.$

...

###### Definition 2.1.

...

A (canonical) hypergroup is a tuple $(ℍ,⊞,𝟘)({\mathbb{H}},\boxplus,{\mathbb{0}})$ where $⊞\boxplus$ is an associative and commutative hyperoperation satisfying:

...

- •

...

(Identity) $𝟘⊞a=a{\mathbb{0}}\boxplus a=a$ for all $a∈ℍa\in{\mathbb{H}}$,
- •

...

(Inverses) For all $a∈ℍa\in{\mathbb{H}}$, there exists a unique $(−a)∈ℍ(-a)\in{\mathbb{H}}$ such that $𝟘∈a⊞−a{\mathbb{0}}\in a\boxplus-a$,
- •

...

(Reversibility) $a∈b⊞ca\in b\boxplus c$ if and only if $c∈a⊞(−b)c\in a\boxplus(-b)$.

...

A hyperring is a tuple $(ℍ,⊞,⊙,𝟘,𝟙)({\mathbb{H}},\boxplus,\odot,{\mathbb{0}},{\mathbb{1}})$, where $⊞\boxplus$ is hyperaddition and $⊙\odot$ is multiplication, satisfying,

...

$(ℍ×,⊙,𝟙)({\mathbb{H}}^{\times},\odot,{\mathbb{1}})$ is a commutative monoid, where $ℍ×:=ℍ∖𝟘{\mathbb{H}}^{\times}:={\mathbb{H}}\setminus{\mathbb{0}}\,$,
- •

...

$a⊙(b⊞c)=a⊙b⊞a⊙ca\odot(b\boxplus c)=a\odot b\boxplus a\odot c$ for all $a,b,c∈ℍa,b,c\in{\mathbb{H}}\quad$ (where $a⊙(b⊞c)=⋃d∈b⊞ca⊙da\odot(b\boxplus c)=\bigcup_{d\in b\boxplus c}a\odot d\,$)
- •

...

$𝟘⊙a=𝟘{\mathbb{0}}\odot a={\mathbb{0}}$ for all $a∈ℍa\in{\mathbb{H}}$.

...

A hyperfield is a hyperring such that $(ℍ,⊙,𝟙)({\mathbb{H}},\odot,{\mathbb{1}})$ is an abelian group, i.e. for every $a∈ℍ×a\in{\mathbb{H}}^{\times}$, there exists a unique element $a−1a^{-1}$ such that $a⊙a−1=𝟙a\odot a^{-1}={\mathbb{1}}$.

For example, consider the univariate polynomials over $𝕊{\mathbb{S}}$:

$f=X2⊞−X⊞𝟙,h=X3⊞X2⊞X⊞𝟙∈(X⊞𝟙)⊡f.f=X^{2}\boxplus-X\boxplus{\mathbb{1}}\,,\quad h=X^{3}\boxplus X^{2}\boxplus X\boxplus{\mathbb{1}}\in(X\boxplus{\mathbb{1}})\boxdot f\,.$
